planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed, setting up a sturdy pole or trellis at planting time since vines climb tall and keep producing over a long season.

directions: This Appalachian heirloom produces smooth, stringless, shiny pods typical of the greasy bean group, with no fuzz on the pod surface. Seeds are notably large and white, and the vines are vigorous, heavy-bearing climbers that benefit from a tall trellis or pole. Pick pods young for snap use or let them mature for shelling and drying. Save seed from fully dry pods for the truest flavor and productivity in following years.

common_name: Red-Striped Greasy Pole Bean (Striped Greasy Cut Short)

planting.note: Sow directly around a sturdy pole or trellis once the soil has warmed, since this vigorous climber needs support from the seedling stage onward.

directions: Pods on this Appalachian heirloom are about five inches long, lightly striped, and smooth-skinned in classic greasy-bean fashion, maturing to mottled brown seed. It is grown both as a quick-cooking snap bean while pods are young and tender, and left to dry fully for a flavorful shelling bean. Vines are long and productive, so plan for a tall support and regular picking to keep pods coming. Flavor is considered a step above ordinary snap beans by many Appalachian growers, which is part of why the greasy-bean tradition persists in home gardens.

planting.note: This is a later-maturing greasy bean, so direct sow as soon as the soil is reliably warm to give the long vines a full season to produce.

directions: A rare Kentucky heirloom from the greasy bean tradition, this variety is named for the gray coloring that rings the eye of an otherwise white seed. Pods are smooth, shiny, and stringless, hanging from tall, heavy-yielding vines that need sturdy staking to support the crop. Being a later-maturing type, it rewards patience with rich, hearty flavor whether cooked fresh or dried for winter use. Because true greasy bean lines are uncommon outside Appalachian seed-saving networks, isolate plantings if you intend to save true seed.

common_name: Granny Bean (Tick Bean, Old-Time Brown Stick, Leer Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow at the base of a pole or trellis after last frost; this comparatively quick-maturing pole bean rewards an early start in the warm-soil window.

directions: Collected from farm families in the Smoky Mountains of Cocke County, Tennessee, this old pole bean produces fat, slightly curved pods over round, brownish-gray seeds. It was traditionally grown both as a canning bean while pods were still fleshy and as a shelled dry bean later in the season. Vines are productive climbers and should be given a tall, sturdy support from planting onward. Its several folk names reflect how widely it was passed hand-to-hand among Appalachian gardeners before formal seed-saving networks preserved it.
